client: I've been really stressed out lately because my final exams are coming up next week and I honestly don't feel ready at all. I've been working so many hours at my part-time job that I barely have time to study, and it feels like everything is just piling up on me. I'm not sure talking about it is actually going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a really heavy load right now — balancing work, exams, and that underlying worry that things might not come together in time. I also notice that even as you describe it, there's a lot of energy and urgency in how you're expressing this, which makes me think the stress might be hitting even harder than your words are letting on. I'm glad you gave this a shot, and I'm curious — when you say you don't feel ready, what does that fear look like for you most?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Honestly, the fear looks like this image I keep getting of sitting down to take the exam and just... going blank. Like everything I should know just disappears, and I end up failing and losing my scholarship, and then I can't afford school anymore and the whole thing falls apart. It's like one bad exam turns into my entire future collapsing, which I know sounds dramatic, but that's genuinely where my brain goes.
therapist: What you're describing actually has a name in CBT — it's called "catastrophizing," where our mind takes one scary possibility and fast-forwards it into a worst-case chain reaction, and it's incredibly common under high stress, so you're not being dramatic at all. That image of going blank is really vivid and painful, and it makes sense that your brain is trying to "protect" you by playing out the worst scenario. I'm wondering — if we slowed that chain down a little, what's the evidence you have, from your past experiences, that you *do* have the ability to handle hard things, even when they feel overwhelming?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I mean, I guess I've gotten through tough semesters before — last year I had three exams in one week and I still passed all of them. But it feels different this time because the job situation wasn't as bad then, and I actually had time to study properly. So I'm not sure that evidence really counts the same way when the circumstances are so much harder now.
therapist: You just did something really interesting — you recalled genuine, concrete evidence of your own resilience, and then almost immediately talked yourself out of it, which tells me your mind is working hard to protect that fear rather than let the good evidence land. That pattern of dismissing your own strengths is worth noticing, because the you who passed three exams in one week is still the same you sitting here today. I'm curious — what would it mean for you if that evidence *did* count, even partially?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess if it counted, it would mean I'm not as helpless as I feel right now, and maybe I have more to work with than I'm giving myself credit for. But honestly, even admitting that feels a little uncomfortable, like I'm setting myself up to be blindsided if things do go wrong this time. It's almost easier to stay in the worst-case mindset because then at least I'm not caught off guard.
therapist: You've just named something really profound — that staying in the worst-case mindset feels like a form of control, a way to protect yourself from being hurt by hope. But I'm noticing that even as you said that, your voice sounded quite soft and tentative, like maybe part of you is carrying more weight around this than the words alone are showing. What do you think it would actually feel like to let yourself believe, even just a little, that you might be okay?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, if I let myself believe I might be okay, I think it would feel like... relief, but also really scary, because then I'd actually have to try my best and still risk failing. Right now the fear kind of gives me an excuse, like if I fail it's because the situation was impossible, not because I wasn't good enough. I think that's what makes it so hard to let go of.
therapist: What you just shared takes a lot of courage and self-awareness — you've identified that the fear isn't just about failing the exam, it's protecting something much deeper, which is your sense of whether you're *good enough*. And the way you said it, quietly and carefully, makes me think this particular fear sits in a really tender place for you. I'm wondering — where do you think that worry about not being good enough first came from?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: That's a hard question, and I'm not sure I want to go too deep into it right now, but I think a lot of it comes from growing up with parents who had really high expectations and where grades were basically how you measured your worth as a person. I got used to the idea that love and approval were kind of conditional on performance, so failing at something has always felt like more than just failing at the thing itself. I guess I never really separated the two.
therapist: What you just shared is really significant — that for you, a grade was never just a grade, it was a measure of whether you were lovable, and that's an incredibly heavy thing to have carried for so long. The way you said it, so quietly and carefully, makes me think this is something you've held close but maybe haven't said out loud very often. I want you to know there's no pressure to go deeper than you're ready for today, but I'm glad you trusted me with that piece — it helps make sense of so much of what you've been describing.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, I don't think I've ever actually said that out loud before, and it feels kind of strange to hear it reflected back at me like that — like it sounds more real now, and I'm not totally sure how I feel about that. It's a little uncomfortable to think that so much of my stress about these exams is tied to something that goes back that far, because it makes it feel even harder to fix. Like, I came in here worried about next week's exams, and now I'm realizing there might be a much bigger thing underneath it all.
therapist: What you're experiencing right now — that strange, slightly unsettling feeling of something becoming more real — is actually a really meaningful moment, and it makes complete sense that it feels like a lot. Discovering a deeper root doesn't make things harder to fix; in many ways it's the opposite, because now you're working on the *actual* problem rather than just the surface symptoms. You came in worried about next week, and that's still real and valid, but what you've uncovered today means that as you do this work, future exams and future high-stakes moments won't have to carry quite so much weight.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that, but I also can't help wondering how any of this actually helps me sit down and study tonight when I get home from work exhausted. Like, understanding where the fear comes from is one thing, but the exams are still happening next week and I still have shifts tomorrow and the day after. I guess I'm just not sure how to bridge the gap between this kind of insight and the very practical, very immediate problem in front of me.
therapist: That's such a fair and important pushback, and you're absolutely right that insight alone doesn't get the studying done. I'm also noticing that even as you said it, there was a kind of urgency in your voice — like the clock is already ticking loudly in the background — so let's make sure you leave today with something concrete. Can we spend a few minutes mapping out one small, realistic study plan for tonight, something that works *with* your exhaustion rather than against it, so that when you sit down you have a clear starting point instead of a blank page?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, okay, I'm willing to try that, but I just want to be honest that when I get home after a long shift I usually just feel kind of numb and the last thing I want to do is open a textbook. I'm a little skeptical that a "small plan" will actually feel doable in that state, because I've told myself before to just study for thirty minutes and then ended up staring at my phone instead. What would make this different from the other times I've tried that?
therapist: That's a really honest and important question, and the fact that you're pushing back on generic advice tells me you know yourself well. The difference this time isn't about willpower — it's about removing the decision-making entirely, because when you're numb and exhausted, even choosing *what* to study becomes its own barrier. So instead of "study for thirty minutes," what if we right now, together, picked one single specific thing — one topic, one set of notes — so that tonight all you have to do is open to a page that's already decided for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Okay, that actually makes a bit of sense to me, because you're right that half the battle is just figuring out where to even start when my brain is already fried. I think the exam I'm most behind on is my statistics one, and there's one specific chapter on regression analysis that I know I'm weak on. So I guess that could be the thing — just opening those notes to that chapter — but I'm still a little worried that even doing that will feel like too much once I'm actually in that moment.
therapist: You've just done something really concrete and useful — you named the exact chapter, which means the decision is already made, and that's genuinely half the battle won before you even get home. I notice though that even as you said it, your voice sounded quite soft and a little drained, like part of you is already feeling the weight of the evening ahead. So let's make the bar even lower — what if tonight the only goal is to open those notes and read just one page, with full permission to stop there if that's all you have?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech
